snippets.content: This paper redevelops Nevanlinna theory for meromorphic functions on C in the viewpoint of holomorphic forms. According to our observation, Nevanlinna's functions can be formulated by a holomorphic form. Applying this thought to Riemann surfaces, one then extends the definition of Nevanlinna's functions using a holomorphic form S. With the new settings, an analogue of Nevanlinna theory for the S-exhausted Riemann surfaces is obtained, which is viewed as a generalization of the classical Nevanlinna theory for C and D.

The paper is motivated by the early work of the first named author [4] (see also Atsuji [1]), who considered Nevanlinna theory for complete Kähler manifolds with nonpositive sectional curvature. To make it simpler, instead of Kähler manifolds, we restrict ourselves to the Riemann surfaces. Let S be a noncompact Riemann surface equipped with a complete Hermitian metric h of nonpositive Gauss curvature K. Fix a reference point o in S. Set k(r) = min{K(x) : x in D(r)}, where D(r) is a geodesic ball of radius r centered at o. Let f be a nonconstant meromorphic function on S. One can well define Nevanlinna's functions T_f(r), m_f(r, a) and N_f(r, a) (see Section 3.1 in [4]). The first named author showed that (see Theorem 1.2 in [4]) for any d > 0, (q - 2)T_f(r) + T(r, R) <= sum_{j=1}^q N_f(r, a_j) + O(log T_f(r) + log C(o, r, d)) holds for all r in (0, infty) outside a set E_d of finite Lebesgue measure, where C(o, r, d) is a positive function with the estimate log C(r, o, d) <= O(r sqrt{-k(r)} + d log r), and the curvature term T(r, R) is bounded by r^2 k(r) <= T(r, R) <= 0. The main drawback of the method in [4] is that the selectivity of metrics is restricted, i.e., the metrics have to be complete and nonpositively curved, but this will result in a rough estimate.

In this paper, we shall investigate Nevanlinna theory from the viewpoint of holomorphic forms S. With this idea, one generalizes the Nevanlinna theory to one class of noncompact Riemann surfaces which we call the S-exhausted Riemann surfaces. To begin with, let us describe how Nevanlinna's functions can be formulated by a holomorphic form S. To see it more clearly, we shall use the Ahlfors' characteristic function T_f(r) = int_1^r dt/t int_{D(t)} f^* omega_FS. Let f be a nonconstant meromorphic function on C. Nevanlinna's characteristic function T(r, f) of f is well known as T(r, f) := m(r, f) + N(r, f), where m(r, f) = int_{|z|=r} log^+ |f| dtheta/(2pi), N(r, f) = int_0^r (n(t, f) - n(0, f))/t dt + n(0, f) log r. Characteristic function is an important notion, it characterizes the growth of meromorphic functions, using which Nevanlinna in 1925 established two fundamental theorems: First Main Theorem and Second Main Theorem, named Nevanlinna theory.

In what follows, we state the main results of the paper. Theorem I (Theorem 3.4), Corollary I, Corollary II, Theorem II (Theorem 4.1), Remark 1.1, and Theorem III. The earlier study of Nevanlinna theory for noncompact Riemann surfaces dates back to the work of H. Wu [17] (also refer to Shabat [16]). More details on this aspect, the readers may refer to the recent very nice papers of He and Ru [7] and Paun and Sibony [13]. We have to indicate that the paper presents a new method of studying Nevanlinna theory by putting a metric h on S. However, we should also point out that our results can be derived by Wu's method (as well as He and Ru's arguments) since S produces an exhaustion function sigma(x) := |int_o^x S| on S, so that log sigma^2 is harmonic outside a compact set.

Theorem I (Theorem 3.4). Let (S, h; S) be a S-exhausted Hermitian Riemann surface of S-radius R^S with respect to o. Let gamma be an integrable function on (0, R^S) with int_0^{R^S} gamma(r) dr = infty. Let f be a nonconstant meromorphic function on S and a_1, ..., a_q be distinct values in C. Then for any d > 0, (q - 2) T_f^S(r) + T^S(r, R) <= sum_{j=1}^q Nbar_f^S(r, a_j) + O(log T_f^S(r) + log ||S||_{r,sup} + log gamma(r) + d log r) holds for all r in (0, R^S) outside a set E_d with int_{E_d} gamma(r) dr < infty, where ||S||_{r,sup} = sup{ ||S_x||_h : |x_hat| < r }.

Corollary I. Let f be a nonconstant meromorphic function on C, and let a_1, ..., a_q be distinct points in C. Then for any d > 0, (q-2) T_f(r) <= sum_{i=1}^q Nbar_f(r, a_j) + O(log T_f(r) + d log r) holds for all r in (0, infty) outside a set E_d of finite Lebesgue measure.

Corollary II. Let f be a nonconstant meromorphic function on D, and let a_1, ..., a_q be distinct points in C. Then for any d > 0, (q-2) T_f(r) <= sum_{i=1}^q Nbar_f(r, a_j) + O(log T_f(r) + log 1/(1-r)) holds for all r in (0, 1) outside a set E_d with int_{E_d} (1-r)^{-1} dr < infty.

Theorem II (Theorem 4.1). Let (S, h; S) be a S-exhausted Hermitian Riemann surface of S-radius R^S with respect to o, and let R be a compact Riemann surface of genus g. Fix a positive (1,1)-form omega on R. Let gamma be an integrable function on (0, R^S) with int_0^{R^S} gamma(r) dr = infty. Let f be a nonconstant holomorphic mapping from S into R and a_1, ..., a_q be distinct points in R. Then for any d > 0, (q - 2 + 2g)T_{f,omega}^S(r) + T^S(r, R) <= sum_{j=1}^q Nbar_f^S(r, a_j) + O(log T_{f,omega}^S(r) + log ||S||_{r,sup} + log gamma(r) + d log r) holds for all r in (0, R^S) outside a set E_d with int_{E_d} gamma(r) dr < infty.

In order to better estimate ||S||, we can put Hermitian metric alpha = sqrt{-1}/2 S wedge Sbar induced by S on S. Under this metric, we have ||S|| equiv 1. Then the result in Theorem II becomes (q - 2 + 2g)T_{f,omega}^S(r) + T^S(r, R) <= sum_{j=1}^q Nbar_f^S(r, a_j) + O(log T_{f,omega}^S(r) + log gamma(r) + d log r).

Theorem III. Assume the same conditions as in Theorem II. Suppose, in addition, that -C <= K <= 0 for a nonnegative constant C. If f satisfies limsup_{r -> R^S} [C r^2 ||S||_{r,inf}^{-1} + log(gamma(r) ||S||_{r,sup})] / T_{f,omega}^S(r) = 0, where ||S||_{r,inf} = inf{ ||S_x||_h : |x_hat| < r }, then we have the defect relation sum_{j=1}^q deltabar_f(a_j) <= 2 - 2g.
Let S be a noncompact Riemann surface. We introduce the concept of S-exhausted Riemann surfaces based on a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic form S satisfying conditions from Gunning and Narasimhan [6].

Proposition 2.1 (Gunning and Narasimhan [6]). Let S be a noncompact Riemann surface. Then there is a holomorphic form S on S satisfying the conditions: (a) S has no zeros on S; (b) int_gamma S = 0 for each smooth simple closed curve gamma in S.

Condition (a) defines a holomorphic field X without zeros on S in the following manner: write S = phi dz in a local holomorphic coordinate z, it is trivial to check that X = phi^{-1} d/dz is well defined on S. Hence, X is a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic field that is dual to S. Condition (b) defines a holomorphic function x_hat : S -> C by L(x) = int_o^x S := x_hat, where o is a fixed point in S. By (a), we see that o is a simple zero of L. In this paper, besides conditions (a) and (b), one assumes that S satisfies an additional condition: L(x) = 0 if and only if x = o. This condition forces L to be a univalent function.

Definition 2.3. Let S be a holomorphic form on S satisfying the conditions (a) and (b) in Proposition 2.1. If, in addition, that S satisfies the condition: L(x) = 0 if and only if x = o, where L is defined by (4), then we say that S is a S-Riemann surface.

Definition 2.4. Let (S; S) be a S-Riemann surface. The S-disc D^S(r) is defined by D^S(r) = {x in S : |x_hat| < r}, and the S-circle C^S(r) is defined by C^S(r) = {x in S : |x_hat| = r}. Since L is univalent, then D^S(r) is simply connected for all r > 0. Notice that the case C^S(r) = empty may happen if r is sufficiently large, since D^S(r) could cover the whole surface S when r is large enough in some situations. For example, we consider the case where S = D and S = dz, then C^S(r) = {z in D : |z| = r}. If r > 1, then we have C^S(r) = empty.

Definition 2.5. We say that S is an exhaustion form, if {D^S(r_n)}_{n=1}^{infty} exhausts S whenever 0 < r_1 < r_2 < ... and r_n -> +infty as n -> +infty. Namely, S = cup_{n=1}^{infty} D^S(r_n) and one of the following holds: (i) D^S(r_1) subset D^S(r_1)-bar subset D^S(r_2) subset D^S(r_2)-bar subset ... subset S. (ii) D^S(r_1) subset D^S(r_1)-bar subset ... subset D^S(r_k) = D^S(r_{k+1}) = ... = S. Precisely, we say that S is a parabolic exhaustion form if condition (i) is satisfied, and a hyperbolic exhaustion form if condition (ii) is satisfied.
Definition 2.6. Let (S; S) be a S-Riemann surface. We say that S is a S-exhausted Riemann surface if S is an exhaustion form on S.

Definition 2.7. Let (S; S) be a S-exhausted Riemann surface. Define R^S by R^S = sup{r > 0 : C^S(r) cap S != empty}, which is called the S-radius of S with respect to o. From the definition as above, we have that 0 < R^S <= infty and C^S(r) is a simple closed curve in S for 0 < r < R^S.

Corollary 2.8. Let (S; S) be a S-exhausted Riemann surface of S-radius R^S with respect to o. Let {r_n}_{n=1}^{infty} be a sequence of positive integers r_n with r_1 < r_2 < ... and r_n -> R^S as n -> +infty. Then {D^S(r_n)}_{n=1}^{infty} exhausts S.

Example 2.9. Let C be the standard complex Euclidean plane, then C is a dz-exhausted Riemann surface of dz-radius infty with respect to 0. We obtain z_hat = z, D^{dz}(r) = {z in C : |z| < r} and C^{dz}(r) = {z in C : |z| = r}.

Example 2.10. Equipping D with standard Euclidean metric, then D is a dz-exhausted Riemann surface of dz-radius 1 with respect to 0. We have z_hat = z, D^{dz}(r) = {z in D : |z| < r} and C^{dz}(r) = {z in D : |z| = r}.

Let (S, h; S) be a S-exhausted Hermitian Riemann surface of S-radius R^S with respect to o. We denote by Delta the Laplace-Beltrami operator on S defined by h. For 0 < r < R^S, we shall compute Green function g_r(o, x) of (1/2)Delta for D^S(r) with Dirichlet boundary and a pole at o, i.e., -(1/2)Delta g_r(o, x) = delta_o(x), x in D^S(r); g_r(o, x) = 0, x in C^S(r) in the sense of distributions, as well as harmonic measure dpi_o^r on C^S(r) with respect to o, for 0 < r < R^S. We have the well-known formula dpi_o^r(x) = -(1/2) dg_r(o, x)/dn dsigma_r(x), where d/dn is the inward normal derivative on C^S(r).
Lemma 2.11. For 0 < r < R^S, we have g_r(o, x) = (1/pi) log(r/|z_hat|).

Proof. Since L is a holomorphic function on S with a unique simple zero o, then it follows that (1/(2pi)) Delta log |L(x)| = delta_o(x), x in D^S(r) in the sense of distribution. Indeed, it is clear that |L(x)| = r for x in C^S(r). Hence, we obtain g_r(o, x) = (1/pi) log(r/|z_hat|). []
Lemma 2.12. For 0 < r < R^S, we have dpi_o^r = (||S||_h)/(2 pi r) dsigma_r, where dsigma_r is the Riemannian line element on C^S(r) defined by h.

Proof. Fix an arbitrary point x_0 in C^S(r), we take a holomorphic coordinate z near x_0 such that h|_{x_0} = 1. Note that dpi_o^r(x) = -(1/2) dg_r(o, x)/dn dsigma_r(x), where d/dn is the inward normal derivative on dC^S(r). By |L(x_0)| = r, we have dpi_o^r(x_0) = (1/(2 pi r)) d|L(x_0)|/dn dsigma_r(x_0). Set z = xi_1 + sqrt{-1} xi_2. Differentiating the equation |L| = r near x_0, then (d|L|/d xi_1) d xi_1 + (d|L|/d xi_2) d xi_2 = 0, which gives an inward normal vector n|_{x_0}. Write S = phi dz in the local coordinate z, a direct computation follows that d|L(x_0)|/d xi_1 = Re[phi(x_0) Lbar(x_0)^{1/2} / L(x_0)^{1/2}], d|L(x_0)|/d xi_2 = -Im[phi(x_0) Lbar(x_0)^{1/2} / L(x_0)^{1/2}]. Then d|L(x_0)|/dn = |phi(x_0)| = ||S_{x_0}||_h. We conclude that dpi_o^r(x_0) = ||S_{x_0}||_h / (2 pi r) dsigma_r(x_0). []

Let (S, h; S) be a S-exhausted Hermitian Riemann surface of S-radius R^S with respect to o. Using S, we extend the notion of Nevanlinna's functions to S. Let f be a meromorphic function on S and let r be satisfied with 0 < r_0 < r < R^S. Viewing f = f_1/f_0 = [f_0 : f_1] as a holomorphic mapping from S into P^1(C). We define the characteristic function of f, proximity function, counting function, and related quantities. We also define the Ricci form R = Ric(alpha) = -dd^c log h, where alpha = sqrt{-1}/pi h dz wedge dzbar is the Kähler form of S. The characteristic of R is defined by T^S(r, R) = int_{r_0}^r dt/t int_{D^S(t)} R. Since the Gauss curvature K of h is computed by K = -(1/2) Delta log h = -(1/h) d^2 log h / (dz d zbar), then we obtain 2R = K alpha. By this with the above, we see that the characteristic of R can be expressed in terms of Gauss curvature: T^S(r, R) = (1/2) int_{D^S(r)} g_r(o, x) K(x) dV(x) - (1/2) int_{D^S(r_0)} g_{r_0}(o, x) K(x) dV(x).
T_f(r) = int_1^r dt/t int_{D(t)} f^* omega_{FS}
m_f(r, a) = int_{|z|=r} log (1/||f, a||) dtheta/(2pi)
deltabar_f(a) = 1 - limsup_{r -> R^S} Nbar_f^S(r, a) / T_{f,omega}^S(r)
L(x) = int_o^x S := x_hat
m_f^S(r, a) = int_{C^S(r)} log (1/||f, a||) dpi_o^r
N_f^S(r, a) = (1/4) int_{D^S(r)} g_r(o, x) Delta log |<f(x); a>|^2 dV(x) - (1/4) int_{D^S(r_0)} g_{r_0}(o, x) Delta log |<f(x); a>|^2 dV(x)
T^S(r, R) = (1/2) int_{D^S(r)} g_r(o, x) K(x) dV(x) - (1/2) int_{D^S(r_0)} g_{r_0}(o, x) K(x) dV(x)
Let us introduce Dynkin formula which is a generalization of Green-Jensen formula [12; 14], see the probabilistic version of Dynkin formula in [4; 8; 9].

Lemma 3.1 (Dynkin formula). Let u be a function of C^2-class except at most a polar set of singularities on a Riemannian manifold M. Let D subset M be a relatively compact domain with piecewise smooth boundary dD. Assume that u(o) != infty for a fixed point o in D. Then int_{dD} u(x) dpi_o^{dD}(x) - u(o) = (1/2) int_D g_D(o, x) Delta u(x) dV(x), where g_D(o, x) is the Green function of Laplacian Delta/2 for D with a pole o and Dirichlet boundary condition, and dpi_o^{dD} is the harmonic measure on dD with respect to o. Here, Delta u is understood as a distribution.

Proof. We are to prove the above lemma by using a probabilistic approach, i.e., the probabilistic Dynkin formula is applied to showing this lemma. Let X_t := {X_t}_{t>=0} be the Brownian motion generated by Delta/2, started at o in M (see Section 2.2 in [4]). Denote by P_o the law or distribution of X_t starting from o and by E_o the expectation of X_t with respect to P_o. Set the stopping time tau_D = inf{t > 0 : X_t notin D}. Note that the probabilistic Dynkin formula (see Ito formula in [4], page 6) says that E_o[u(X_{tau_D})] - u(o) = (1/2) E_o[int_0^{tau_D} Delta u(X_t) dt]. On the other hand, using the co-area formula (see (2) in [4]) and the relation between harmonic measures and hitting times (see (3) in [4]), we obtain E_o[int_0^{tau_D} Delta u(X_t) dt] = int_D g_D(o, x) Delta u(x) dV(x) and E_o[u(X_{tau_D})] = int_{dD} u(x) dpi_o^{dD}(x). Substituting the two equalities into the above probabilistic Dynkin formula, we have the lemma proved. []
Theorem 3.2 (First Main Theorem). If f notequiv a, then we have T_f^S(r) = m_f^S(r, a) + N_f^S(r, a) + O(1).

Theorem 3.2 can be confirmed by using Green-Jensen formula instead of Dynkin formula, since S can produce a parabolic or a hyperbolic exhaustion function sigma(x) = |int_o^x S|; see, e.g., [7; 13; 16; 17].
The main purpose here is to prove the following theorem.

Theorem 3.4 (Second Main Theorem). Let (S, h; S) be a S-exhausted Hermitian Riemann surface of S-radius R^S with respect to o. Let gamma be an integrable function on (0, R^S) with int_0^{R^S} gamma(r) dr = infty. Let f be a nonconstant meromorphic function on S and a_1, ..., a_q be distinct values in C. Then for any d > 0, (q - 2)T_f^S(r) + T^S(r, R) <= sum_{j=1}^q N_f^S(r, a_j) + O(log T_f^S(r) + log ||S||_{r,sup} + log gamma(r) + d log r) holds for all r in (0, R^S) outside a set E_d with int_{E_d} gamma(r) dr < infty, where ||S||_{r,sup} = sup{||S_x||_h : |x_hat| < r}.

Lemma 3.5 [15]. Let gamma be an integrable function on (0, R) with int_0^R gamma(r) dr = infty. Let h be a nondecreasing function of C^1-class on (0, R). Let lim_{r -> R} h(r) = infty and h(r_0) > 0 for some r_0 in (0, R). Then for any d > 0, h'(r) <= h^{1+d}(r) gamma(r) holds for all r in (0, R) outside a set E_d with int_{E_d} gamma(r) dr < infty. In particular, when R = infty, we can take gamma = 1. Then for any d > 0, h'(r) <= h^{1+d}(r) holds for all r in (0, infty) outside a set E_d of finite Lebesgue measure.

Lemma 3.6. Let (S, h; S) be a S-exhausted Hermitian Riemann surface of S-radius R^S with respect to o. Let gamma be an integrable function on (0, R^S) with int_0^{R^S} gamma(r) dr = infty. Let k be a locally integrable function on S. Then for any d > 0, E_k(r) <= (||S||_{r,sup} r^d gamma^{2+d}(r) / (2 pi)) A_k^{(1+d)^2}(r) holds for all r in (0, R^S) outside a set E_d with int_{E_d} gamma(r) dr < infty, where ||S||_{r,sup} = sup{||S_x||_h : |x_hat| < r}.

Proof (Lemma 3.6). Notice that int_{D^S(r)} k dV = int_0^r dt int_{C^S(t)} k dsigma_r, then it follows from Lemma 2.12 that d/dr (r dA_k/dr) = int_{C^S(r)} k dsigma_r >= (2 pi r / ||S||_{r,sup}) E_k(r). Using Lemma 3.5 twice (first to rA_k' and then to A_k), we obtain E_k(r) <= (||S||_{r,sup} r^d gamma^{2+d}(r) / (2 pi)) A_k^{(1+d)^2}(r). []

Proof of Theorem 3.4. Consider a singular volume form (see [2; 5]) Phi = C omega_{FS} / (prod_{j=1}^q ||zeta, a_j||^2 log^2 ||zeta, a_j||^{-2}) on Cbar, where a_1, ..., a_q are distinct values in Cbar and omega_{FS} = dd^c log(1 + |zeta|^2). Since Cbar is compact, we can choose a positive number C such that int_{Cbar} Phi = 1. Set f^* Phi = xi (sqrt{-1}/pi) h dz wedge dzbar. By taking the Ricci form of both sides of the above identity, it follows from Ric(omega_{FS}) = 2 omega_{FS} that dd^c[log xi] = (q - 2) f^* omega_{FS} - sum_{j=1}^q (f - a_j)_0 + D_{f,ram} + R - 2 sum_{j=1}^q dd^c log log ||f, a_j||^{-2} in the sense of currents, where (f - a_j)_0 is the zero divisor of f - a_j, D_{f,ram} is the ramification divisor of f, and R = -dd^c log h is the Ricci form of S. Applying the integral operator int_{r_0}^r dt/t int_{D^S(t)} to the above identity and using Dynkin formula, we get (1/2) int_{C^S(r)} log xi dpi_o^r = (q-2) T_f^S(r) - sum_{j=1}^q N_f^S(r, a_j) + N^S(r, D_{f,ram}) + T^S(r, R) - sum_{j=1}^q int_{C^S(r)} log log ||f, a_j||^{-2} dpi_o^r + O(1) >= (q-2) T_f^S(r) - sum_{j=1}^q Nbar_f^S(r, a_j) + T^S(r, R) - sum_{j=1}^q int_{C^S(r)} log log ||f, a_j||^{-2} dpi_o^r + O(1). The concavity of log implies that int_{C^S(r)} log log ||f, a_j||^{-2} dpi_o^r <= log int_{C^S(r)} log ||f, a_j||^{-2} dpi_o^r = log m_f^S(r, a_j) + O(1) <= log T_f^S(r) + O(1). By this, we obtain (1/2) int_{C^S(r)} log xi dpi_o^r >= (q-2) T_f^S(r) - sum_{j=1}^q Nbar_f^S(r, a_j) + T^S(r, R) + O(log T_f^S(r)) + O(1). It remains to estimate the upper bound. By Lemma 3.6, for any d > 0, int_{C^S(r)} log xi dpi_o^r <= log int_{C^S(r)} xi dpi_o^r <= (1+d)^2 log int_{r_0}^r dt/t int_{D^S(t)} xi dV + log ||S||_{r,sup} + (2+d) log gamma(r) + d log r + O(1) = (1+d)^2 log int_{r_0}^r dt/t int_{D^S(t)} f^*Phi + log ||S||_{r,sup} + (2+d) log gamma(r) + d log r + O(1). Notice that int_{D^S(r)} f^*Phi = int_C n_f^S(r, zeta) Phi(zeta) due to the change of variable formula. Using Fubini theorem, then int_{r_0}^r dt/t int_{D^S(t)} f^*Phi = int_C N_f^S(r, zeta) Phi(zeta) <= c_0 T_f^S(r) for some positive constant c_0. Combining the above, we conclude that int_{C^S(r)} log xi dpi_o^r <= (1+d)^2 log T_f^S(r) + log ||S||_{r,sup} + (2+d) log gamma(r) + d log r + O(1). Put together the lower and upper bounds, then we prove the theorem. []

int_{C^S(r)} log xi dpi_o^r <= (1+d)^2 log T_f^S(r) + log ||S||_{r,sup} + (2+d) log gamma(r) + d log r + O(1)

Corollary 3.8. Assume the same conditions as in Theorem 3.4. Suppose, in addition, that -C <= K <= 0 for a nonnegative constant C. If f satisfies limsup_{r -> R^S} [C r^2 ||S||_{r,inf}^{-1} + log(gamma(r) ||S||_{r,sup})] / T_f^S(r) = 0, then we have the defect relation sum_{j=1}^q deltabar_f(a_j) <= 2. Theorem 3.7. Assume the same conditions as in Theorem 3.4. Suppose, in addition, that -C <= K <= 0 for a nonnegative constant C. In a local holomorphic coordinate zeta, we may write omega as omega = (sqrt{-1}/(2 pi)) w d zeta wedge d zetabar. According to Chern's theorem [3], we have that for every a in R, there exists a positive function u_a on R such that 2 dd^c[log u_a] = omega - delta_a, where delta_a should be understood as a current. Let f : S -> R be a holomorphic mapping. For a in R with f notequiv a, by replacing ||f, a||^{-1} by u_a circ f, we define similarly the Nevanlinna's functions. We need to modify the singular volume form Phi for the higher genus case. If g = 0, then R can be regarded as P^1(C). Since C_1 omega_{FS} <= omega <= C_2 omega_{FS} for two suitable positive constants, then we can confirm the theorem by using the conclusion proved in Theorem 3.4. In the following, we assume that g >= 1.

snippets.content: Theorem 4.1. Let (S, h; S) be a S-exhausted Hermitian Riemann surface of S-radius R^S with respect to o, and R be a compact Riemann surface of genus g. Fix a positive (1,1)-form omega on R. Let gamma be an integrable function on (0, R^S) with int_0^{R^S} gamma(r) dr = infty. Let f : S -> R be a nonconstant holomorphic mapping and a_1, ..., a_q be distinct points in R. Then for any d > 0, (q-2+2g) T_{f,omega}^S(r) + T^S(r, R) <= sum_{j=1}^q Nbar_f^S(r, a_j) + O(log T_{f,omega}^S(r) + log ||S||_{r,sup} + log gamma(r) + d log r) holds for all r in (0, R^S) outside a set E_d with int_{E_d} gamma(r) dr < infty, where ||S||_{r,sup} = sup{ ||S_x||_h : |x_hat| < r }.

Theorem 4.2 derives a defect relation, i.e., Theorem III in Introduction.
